newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries seen profiting from EMU jitters.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries seen profiting from EMU jitters.

text.p: The short-term outlook for dollar-denominated assets is seen bright, as investors look for shelter from recent political uncertainty surrounding the adoption of a single currency in Europe, U.S. experts said.
"The Treasury market still looks relatively cheap, given the uncertainty in European countries," said Richard Gilhooly, international bond strategist at Paribas Capital Markets.
"You'll see spreads widening in Europe and you'll see Treasuries outperform, but probably outperforming high yielders rather than Germany," he added.

Analysts said players have been drawn to the safety of U.S. Treasuries as recent events in Europe raised doubts about the timing of the implementation of the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), scheduled for January 1, 1999.

Bond experts said the spread between U.S. and German interest rates has thinned markedly in recent weeks and Treasuries may have more scope to appreciate against European debt, especially versus instruments like Italian BTPs.

U.S. investors have already started unwinding convergence trades, paring holdings of financial instruments from countries such as Italy, Spain, even Germany, whose yields had become relatively more attractive compared with U.S. bonds, they said. Much of these proceeds went back into U.S. Treasury securities, global experts said.
Such a transition, however, is not likely to translate into a one-to-one boost for the U.S. currency.
"Most of that money is American money, which was in overseas markets and had already been hedged into dollars in any case," Gilhooly said.
"So, as hedges unwind you see the dollar weakening from that point of view as well. It's not necessarily money which is coming into dollars and coming into Treasuries," he added.

Experts said that as bond managers reallocate back into Treasuries, some also need to unwind dollar hedges set previously to protect themselves from possible depreciation of the underlying high yielders.
In the 10-year horizon, spreads of U.S. yields over bunds have already narrowed over the last two months from 120 basis point to below 80 currently, analysts said.

Differentials in the 10-year maturity were roughly 95 basis points before the recent French election two weeks ago, they said. The election of a Socialist-led government in France and its subsequent foot-dragging on passing a key feature of Europe's proposed single currency sent shudders through European financial markets.

On Monday, the new French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said France needed more time to consider the stability pact, negotiated in December to enshrine fiscal discipline among member nations after the scheduled launch of EMU in 1999.

The French decision seemed to derail the planned approval of the pact at next week's European Union summit in Amsterdam and sparked a rally in the mark and an immediate shakeout in French markets amidst fears the whole project would be postponed. But on consideration, most strategists predicted EMU would still go ahead on time, although with a diluted euro, as France holds out for broader membership.
"To the extent people think the new European union is going to be 'deutschemark light,' that is going to be bad for German assets," said Josh Feinman, global markets economist at Bankers Trust.
"To the extent they think it's not going to happen at all, then it's going to be good for German assets," he added.
The odds of a delay, however, are increasing, they said. This would immediately re-anchor the German mark and the Bundesbank as the core of Europe, they said.

"You've got the strong currency and the Bundesbank, the world's most credible central bank, so I would think that would be a modest negative on Treasuries and perhaps a significant negative for dollar/mark, if the thing cancels," said Richard Koss, international strategist at MFR Inc.
"If it goes ahead, then visa versa. In the meantime, I'd say Treasuries will benefit a little bit until you're sure."
